qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lecture sixteen. Neural networks. Simple neurons, joined by adjustable weights, that learn instead of following rules.
Meet Nell, the flood warden of Mossbrook. Her calculator multiplies two four-digit numbers in a flash.
A calculator multiplies huge numbers in a flash.
It also recalls an exact time from years ago, and keeps it for ever.
It also recalls exact facts for ever.
But catching a ball, or spotting a face in a blurry image, defeats it. Nell does both without thinking.
But catching a ball or spotting a face? You win.
A computer works step by step. A brain is distributed. It learns, generalises, and forgets.
Brains are distributed: they learn, generalise and forget.
The brain has about a hundred billion neurons.
Your brain holds about 100 billion neurons.
Each one is connected to around ten thousand others.
Each one links to around 10,000 others.
They meet at synapses. Like a volume knob, a synapse can turn the next neuron up, which is excite, or down, which is inhibit.
A synapse can excite or inhibit, like a volume knob.
A synapse can also be strengthened. That change is thought to be where learning happens.
Synapses can be strengthened: that is where learning lives.
Nell's rulebook says, if rain is over twenty millimetres and the ground is wet, warn. That is symbolic AI.
Symbolic AI: an expert types in IF-THEN rules.
It is easy to read. But a storm of nineteen millimetres on soaked ground slips straight past it.
Easy to read, but fragile outside its scope.
Connectionism instead learns numbers, called weights, in a network of simple units.
Connectionism learns numbers, called weights, in a network.
It generalises and fails gracefully, but it is a black box. It is hard to say why it answered.
It generalises and fails gracefully, but is a black box.
A real neuron receives through its dendrites, decides in the cell body, and transmits along its axon.
A neuron listens, decides, and passes it on.
McCulloch and Pitts, in nineteen forty-three, multiply each input by a weight and add them up.
McCulloch and Pitts, 1943: inputs times weights, then add.
Two clears a threshold of one point five, so it fires. Only both inputs together do that. This is AND.
1 + 1 = 2 clears a threshold of 1.5, so it fires. That is AND.
Drop the threshold to nought point five, and one input is enough. Now it is OR.
Lower the threshold to 0.5: one input is enough. OR.
With weights of minus one and a threshold of minus one point five, the inputs inhibit. This is NAND.
Negative weights inhibit: weights −1, threshold −1.5 give NAND.
Nell's canal lock has two gates. Its lamp should glow when exactly one gate is open.
Nell's lock lamp should glow when exactly one gate is open.
That rule is XOR, exclusive or. Its on cases sit in opposite corners.
That rule is XOR. Its 'on' cases sit in opposite corners.
One neuron can only split the square with one straight line.
One neuron draws one straight line.
Wherever the line goes, a corner lands on the wrong side. One neuron cannot compute XOR.
No straight line separates XOR. One neuron can't do it.
The fix is a hidden layer. An OR neuron and a NAND neuron both feed an AND neuron.
Add a hidden layer: OR and NAND feed an AND.
With both gates shut, OR stays silent. With both open, NAND stays silent. So the output stays dark.
0 0 and 1 1: the hidden pair disagree, so no light.
With exactly one gate open, both fire, so the output fires.
0 1 and 1 0: both agree, so the output fires.
Three neurons, two layers, and XOR is solved.
That is XOR from three neurons.
This is the multi-layer perceptron, made famous by Rumelhart and McClelland in nineteen eighty-six.
The multi-layer perceptron: Rumelhart and McClelland, 1986.
Nell's rain brain has twenty hidden neurons. Its fit score is nought point nine nine.
Nell's rain brain: 20 hidden neurons, fit score 0.99.
Lightning knocks out neuron seven. The curve dips, and the score falls to nought point eight three.
Lightning knocks out neuron 7. Fit score 0.83.
Pull one wire from a rule system, and it usually stops working altogether.
Pull one wire from a rule system and it usually fails.
The network only loses some performance. That is graceful degradation.
That is graceful degradation.
Because it learned patterns, it also copes with new cases and noise.
Learned patterns also generalise to new cases and noise.
Now the case study. The network takes rainfall and air temperature, and predicts sewer flow.
The case study: rainfall and temperature in, sewer flow out.
The data cover fifteen rainfall events, from January twenty ten to October twenty twelve.
15 rainfall events, January 2010 to October 2012.
Each split holds one storm back for testing. That is cross-validation.
Cross-validation: each split holds one storm back for testing.
An evolutionary algorithm trains it. Each individual is one complete set of weights.
Train with an EA: each solution is a complete set of weights.
Fitness is the mean absolute error. The best starts at nought point four zero seven.
Fitness is the mean absolute error, MAE. Start: 0.407.
Crossover mixes two parents, and mutation nudges one weight by a little Gaussian noise.
Mutation adds small Gaussian noise to one weight.
At generation twenty, the error is nought point nought seven two, and the Nash-Sutcliffe score nought point nine two.
Generation 20: MAE 0.072, Nash-Sutcliffe 0.92.
By generation fifty it reaches nought point nine nine. The error fell fast at first, then slowly.
Generation 50: NSE 0.99. Fast at first, then slow.
On that scale, one is perfect, guessing the average scores nought, and there is no lower limit.
NSE: best 1, guessing the average scores 0, no lower limit.
A neuron weighs its inputs and fires at its threshold.
One hidden layer can compute XOR, which one neuron cannot.
Networks degrade gracefully, and evolution can tune their weights.
